specAnchors.text: know what is meant by the terms: solvent, solute, solution, saturated solution

primer.text: Everyday life already teaches this note: stirring sugar into tea or salt into soup shows something vanishing into a liquid. That liquid, that vanished substance and the resulting mixture each carry a precise name, and this note fixes the vocabulary — solvent, solute, solution, saturated solution, soluble, insoluble — using sea water, where all of them appear at once.

modules.title: Solutions Terminology
modules.opening: Dissolving has a vocabulary of its own, and every term in it names a role. Sea water carries the whole set in one example: the water is the solvent, the salt is the solute, and the mixture itself is the solution. Add enough salt and the water refuses to take more — the saturated state — which the Dead Sea shows on a grand scale.
keyPoints: The solvent is the liquid doing the dissolving; in sea water it is the water.
The solute is the substance that dissolves; in sea water it is the salt.
A solution is the mixture formed once a solute has dissolved in a solvent.
A saturated solution holds the maximum amount of dissolved solute the solvent can take, as with sea water in the Dead Sea.
Soluble describes a substance that will dissolve, and insoluble describes one that will not, like sand in water.

low.restatement: Six terms describe dissolving. The solvent is the liquid, the solute is what dissolves in it, and the solution is the mixture you get; saturated means no more solute can dissolve, while soluble and insoluble record whether something dissolves at all.
low.analogy: Making a cup of tea: the hot water is the solvent, the sugar is the solute, the sweet drink is the solution — and once sugar piles up undissolved at the bottom, the cup is saturated.
low.examPointer: Definition questions are free marks when the terms are precise: learn each one with its single-line meaning and a sea-water example.

medium.restatement: In a solution the solvent is the liquid doing the dissolving and the solute is the substance dissolved in it; the solution is the mixture that results. A saturated solution carries the greatest amount of dissolved solute possible, and soluble or insoluble records whether a substance will dissolve.
medium.analogy: A rush-hour bus: the bus is the solvent, the passengers are the solute, the loaded bus is the solution, and when nobody else can board, it is saturated.
medium.examPointer: Expect a match-the-term item or a definition with a missing word; quote the term exactly (saturated solution, not saturated liquid) and attach the sea-water or Dead Sea example where it fits.

glossary.definition: The liquid that does the dissolving; in sea water the solvent is the water.
The substance that dissolves in the liquid; in sea water the solute is the salt.
The mixture formed once a solute has dissolved in a solvent; sea water is the example.
A solution holding the greatest amount of dissolved solute the solvent can take, such as sea water in the Dead Sea.
Describing a substance that is able to dissolve, like salt in water.
Describing a substance that is unable to dissolve, like sand in water.

workedExample.prompt: A learner stirs salt and sand into a beaker of water. The salt disappears into the water but the sand settles on the bottom. Name: a) the role of the water, b) the role of the salt, c) the mixture formed once the salt has dissolved, d) the term describing the sand.
steps: a) The water is the solvent: the liquid doing the dissolving.
b) The salt is the solute: the substance that dissolves in the liquid to form the mixture.
c) Once the solute has dissolved in the solvent, the mixture is called the solution.
d) The sand does not dissolve, so it is insoluble.
workedExample.finalAnswer: a) Solvent. b) Solute. c) Solution. d) Sand is insoluble.
